Surface area:
Surface area is the total area of all the faces of a solid. It is measured in square units such as cm^2.

Cuboid with length l, width w, height h: S = 2(lw + lh + wh). Cube with edge a: S = 6a^2. Prism: S = 2 × (base area) + (base perimeter) × h. Cylinder with radius r and height h: S = 2πr^2 + 2πrh. Cone with slant height s: S = πr^2 + πrs, where s^2 = r^2 + h^2. Sphere: S = 4πr^2.

To find the area, imagine unfolding the solid into a flat shape called a net, then add the areas of its parts.
Volume of solids:
Volume is the amount of space inside a solid. It is measured in cubic units such as cm^3.

Prism or cylinder: V = (base area) × h. Cuboid: V = lwh. Cube: V = a^3. Cylinder: V = πr^2h. Pyramid or cone: V = 1/3 × (base area) × h, so a cone has V = 1/3 πr^2h. Sphere: V = 4/3 πr^3.

A cone or pyramid has exactly one third of the volume of a prism or cylinder with the same base and height. Always use the same unit for all lengths before you calculate.
Cross sections:
A cross section is the shape you see when a plane cuts through a solid. The shape depends on the solid and on the direction of the cut.

A cube cut parallel to a face gives a square. A cylinder cut parallel to its bases gives a circle, and cut through its axis gives a rectangle. A cone cut parallel to its base gives a smaller circle, and cut through its apex and axis gives a triangle. Every cross section of a sphere is a circle.

If a plane is at distance d from the center of a sphere of radius R, the circle has radius r = √(R^2 - d^2).
Solids of revolution:
A solid of revolution is made by turning a flat shape around a straight line, called the axis, for one full turn.

A rectangle turned about one of its sides gives a cylinder. A right triangle turned about one of its legs gives a cone. A semicircle turned about its diameter gives a sphere. A circle turned about its diameter also gives a sphere.

To find the radius and height of the new solid, look at the distance of the shape from the axis and the length of the shape along the axis. Then use the volume and surface area formulas for that solid.
